title: Comments of EDF Power Solutions, Inc. re Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.'s 09/21/2026 Legacy Queue Acceleration Proposal under ER26-3813.

documents.name: EDFps Comments ER26-3813.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.                        Docket No. ER26-3813-000

                        COMMENTS OF EDF POWER SOLUTIONS, INC.
          Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (Commission or FERC), 1 EDF power solutions, Inc. (EDFps)

respectfully submits these comments regarding the Legacy Queue Acceleration Proposal filed by

the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) on September 21, 2026 (the LQA

Proposal). 2

I.        SUMMARY OF COMMENTS
          MISO’s LQA Proposal advances the important goal of accelerating the resolution of its

largest and most delayed legacy queue. EDFps supports MISO’s proposed one-time, penalty-

free withdrawal opportunity at Decision Point II (DP2), and the increased 50% penalty-free

withdrawal threshold that applies once DP2 concludes for the Definitive Planning Process (DPP)

2022 Cycle. EDFps further supports, in tandem with other efforts, the corresponding limit of one

final restudy in Phase III for DPP-2022 and all subsequent DPP cycles. These provisions are

appropriately tailored to the scale and maturity of DPP-2022 and will provide MISO the tools it

needs to help bring this Cycle to a close.




1
    18 C.F.R. § 385.213 (2025).
2
  Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Legacy Queue Acceleration Proposal and Request for
Expedited Action, Shortened Comment Period, and Waiver of the Sixty-Day Prior Notice Requirement,
Docket No. ER26-3813 (Sept. 21, 2026). MISO proposes to (1) grant Interconnection Customers a one-
time opportunity to withdraw penalty-free at DP2 from the DPP-2022 Cycle; (2) increase the Network
Upgrades threshold for the purposes of penalty-free withdrawal from thirty-five percent (35%) to fifty
percent (50%) for Interconnection Customers who withdraw post-DP2; and (3) limit the number of Phase
III Interconnection Restudies for all DPP cycles, including DPP-2022, to one restudy.
        MISO’s LQA Proposal is a step in the right direction. By itself, however, it will not

resolve the backlog because not all delays in MISO’s interconnection queue are attributable to

late-stage withdrawals. Three DPP Cycles – 2022, 2023, and 2025 – currently sit in Phase II

simultaneously. MISO should prioritize completing its oldest cycles before advancing newer

ones. In addition, facility studies, which have in some instances taken 15 to 18 months to

complete, are another source of delay in projects achieving study completion that undermines the

accuracy of the Phase III System Impact Study (SIS) results for the subsequent cycle.

Interconnection Customers must now rely more heavily on these results as there will only be one

chance to withdraw penalty-free following the first Phase III SIS. Thus, MISO should also aim

to ensure the TOs can accelerate their facility studies to be completed within the tariff specified

duration of 90 calendar days.

       For these reasons, the Commission should approve the LQA Proposal and direct MISO to

adopt project management measures to separate and prioritize older DPP cycles and improve the

timeliness of transmission facility studies. Without these further steps, the LQA Proposal will

fall short of its goal to resolve the delays that continue to burden MISO’s interconnection queue.

II.    BACKGROUND
       EDFps develops, builds, operates, and manages renewable energy projects throughout

North America, including in CAISO, MISO, NYISO, PJM, SPP and ERCOT. EDFps also

develops such projects in non-RTO regions of the United States and in Canada. As a market-

leading independent power producer and service provider for over 35 years, EDFps delivers grid-

scale power, including wind (onshore and offshore), solar photovoltaic, and storage projects;

distribution-scale power, including solar and storage, and asset optimization. The company also

provides technical, operational, and commercial expertise to maximize performance of




                                                 2
 generating projects. EDFps is an active participant in interconnection and large load-related

policy discussions, rulemaking proceedings and reform efforts.

III.      COMMENTS

          A.      MISO’s Proposed Penalty-Free Withdrawal Opportunity and One-Restudy
                  Limit for DPP-2022 Should be Accepted Subject to Clarification.
          EDFps supports the targeted approach providing for penalty-free withdrawal at DP2 for the

DPP-2022 Cycle, combined with a limit of a single Phase III restudy. As proposed, an

Interconnection Customer in the DPP-2022 Cycle that withdraws its Interconnection Request prior

to the conclusion of DP2 will receive an unconditional, one hundred percent (100%) refund of its

entry milestone payment. In exchange, an Interconnection Customer that elects to remain in the

queue beyond DP2 will be faced with an increase in the cost threshold of Network Upgrades for

the purpose of penalty-free withdrawal from 35% to 50%, together with an increase of $15,000 per

MW, to qualify for penalty-free withdrawal thereafter. The LQA Proposal further limits MISO to

one final Interconnection Study restudy after Phase III commences, applicable to DPP-2022 and all

subsequent DPP cycles, if a restudy is necessary to ensure Transmission System reliability. These

proposed changes are well-founded. MISO’s filing recognizes that absent reform, DPP-2022

(MISO’s largest cycle to date) is likely to experience the same cascading withdrawals and

recurrent restudies that have plagued prior cycles, only on a larger scale. 3

          EDFps also agrees with MISO’s observation that the current withdrawal-penalty

framework has worked against its own purpose by incentivizing some unviable projects to

remain in the queue longer than would otherwise have occurred because Interconnection

Customers are not compelled to withdraw until they qualify for penalty-free exit. 4 The LQA



3
    LQA Proposal at 4, 6.
4
    Id. at 13.


                                                  3
 Proposal’s combination of a one-time incentive to exit and a more meaningful deterrent for those

who remain appropriately address this issue for the DPP-2022 Cycle and will help alleviate the

overall queue backlog.

          EDFps recognizes that this approach is not without cost to Interconnection Customers.

An Interconnection Customer in DPP-2022 that elects to remain in the queue past DP2 will be

giving up the protection currently available under the 35% Network Upgrade cost increase

threshold upon completion of the Phase III study. Also, an Interconnection Customer in all

cycles yet to complete a Phase III study could face a significant cost increase arising from the

single permitted Phase III restudy with no further opportunity to withdraw penalty-free if that

restudy produces an adverse result. On balance, however, given the current state of the ongoing

DPP Cycles and the risk of prolonged, cascading restudies under the status quo, EDFps believes

the benefits of this approach – namely, finality for the DPP-2022 and later cycles – outweigh this

drawback.

          EDFps requests one clarification to ensure the LQA Proposal is implemented as intended.

MISO proposes creating a new Section 5.15 “Transition of Legacy Queue Cycles” to its

Attachment X, Generator Interconnection Procedures (GIP). This Section establishes the 50%

Network Upgrade cost-increase threshold specific to the DPP-2022 Cycle for penalty-free

withdrawal after DP2. The Tariff’s existing penalty-free withdrawal provision, Section 7.6.2.4

of the GIP, governs the threshold generally applicable based on Phase II-to-Phase III cost

increases, but does not appear to cross-reference the DPP-2022-specific exception established in

Section 5.15. 5 To avoid ambiguity or an apparent conflict between these two provisions, EDFps




5
    MISO FERC Electric Tariff, Attachment X, GIP, Section 7.6.2.4.


                                                    4
 respectfully requests that the Commission direct MISO to revise Section 7.6.2.4 of the GIP to

expressly cross-reference the Section 5.15 exception applicable to the DPP-2022 Cycle.

       Subject to this clarification, EDFps supports acceptance of these provisions. As

discussed below, however, these measures respond only to delays driven by withdrawal and

restudies. They do not address other significant sources of delay within MISO’s interconnection

queue, which EDFps addresses in the following sections.

       B.      MISO Should Prioritize Cycle Separation to Preserve the Accuracy of Phase
               III Study Results.
       The LQA Proposal does not address the delays caused by the lack of separation between

successive DPP cycles. MISO’s filing confirms that the DPP-2022 and DPP-2023 Cycles’ Phase

II studies are proceeding, or will proceed, in parallel following the conclusion of DP2. 6 This

overlap – compounded further by the ongoing DPP-2025 Cycle – illustrates that MISO’s cycle-

processing sequence lacks the separation necessary to ensure reliable study results, and it

undermines the need for accuracy that the LQA Proposal depends upon to function as intended.

       Cycle separation matters more now that the LQA Proposal limits Interconnection

Customers to a single opportunity to withdraw penalty-free following the one permitted Phase III

restudy. MISO’s filing acknowledges that a restudy in a single study region necessarily delays

an entire cycle, and that withdrawals of higher-queued Interconnection Customers – including

those with effective Generator Interconnection Agreements (GIAs) – can trigger restudies in

lower-queued cycles. 7 When cycles run in parallel rather than in sequence, Interconnection

Customers face a greater risk that a still-open, higher-queued cycle will force a restudy of their



6
  LQA Proposal at 10 (noting Transmission Owners’ concerns regarding the timing of DP2, and that
completion of DP2 “will allow both the DPP-2022 and DPP-2023 Phase II studies [to] proceed in
parallel.”).
7
  Id. at 3.


                                                  5
 own cycle’s results. 8 Because MISO will no longer correct these inaccuracies for DPP-2022

through additional restudies or withdrawals, the quality of the first and only Phase III study is

now critical to the LQA Proposal working as intended.

       MISO should therefore prioritize processing its oldest open cycles to completion before

advancing newer ones and thereby avoid completing Phase III studies for a cycle until

completion of all earlier-queued cycles. Doing so will ensure that, by the time a cycle receives

its final Phase III SIS report, its study is based on final information. This will reduce the

uncertainty in Phase III results at the same time the LQA Proposal removes Interconnection

Customers’ ability to withdraw penalty-free after an adverse restudy outcome. MISO’s filing

recognizes that predictable study timelines, particularly in Phase III, are critical not only to

resolving DPP-2022 but to all future cycles. 9

       EDFps requests that the Commission direct MISO to accelerate its existing commitment

to a defined cycle-separation policy, prioritizing completion of its oldest legacy cycles and

avoiding further overlap between concurrent DPP cycles going forward. As an example of this

existing commitment, Section 3.3.1 of the Tariff provides that the Phase I application deadline

for the next cycle cannot close until after 45 calendar days following the close of DP2 of the

prior cycle. 10 While Section 3.3.1 applies to the start of a new cycle following completion of

Phase II of the prior cycle, a similar separation would have a comparable effect if applied to

Phase III. This gap between cycle application deadlines demonstrates that MISO already treats

cycle separation as a necessary tool for achieving study timelines. The LQA Proposal makes that



8
  Id.
9
  Id. at 16.
10
   MISO FERC Electric Tariff, Attachment X, GIP, Section 3.3.1.



                                                  6
 separation even more important because it allows only one restudy in Phase III for DPP-2022

and one penalty-free withdrawal following Phase III SIS. MISO should make every effort to

extend this cycle-separation practice going forward and FERC should hold MISO accountable

for doing so.

          C.     MISO Must Address Chronic Delays in Transmission Facility Studies.
          A second, unaddressed source of queue backlog is the persistent delays of transmission

facility studies. Facility studies have in some cases taken more than 18 months to complete –

well beyond the timeline specified in the Tariff. These delays often prevent an affected

Interconnection Customer from knowing whether its project is viable so that it can execute a

GIA, Facilities Construction Agreement (FCA), or Multi-Parties Facilities Construction

Agreement (MPFCA). The LQA Proposal’s tariff revisions are not enough to correct this

problem. MISO must devote adequate staffing resources to track and enforce the progress of

these studies in the legacy cycles to ensure timely completion.

          Interconnection Customers can withdraw penalty-free if facility study costs turn out to be

significantly higher than the Phase III SIS estimated. 11 But this option only helps once the

facility study is done. It does nothing to reduce the uncertainty Interconnection Customers face

while that study remains outstanding. Also, delayed facility studies can delay agreement

negotiation and execution for a given cycle, affecting confidence in the Phase III results in the

next study cycle, compounding the accuracy concerns discussed in Section III.B above. These

concerns are now heightened given that Interconnection Customers will have only one

opportunity to withdraw after the Phase III SIS without facing a penalty. 12 MISO’s proposal is

not clear on this point. In certain cases, a subsequent evaluation may be warranted and may


11
     LQA Proposal at 10.
12
     Id. at 10-11.


                                                  7
 benefit the projects remaining in the queue. Instead, MISO should be required to explain in

greater detail the mechanics of any such subsequent evaluation. This explanation should address

how it will handle the portfolio of projects remaining after the one permitted withdrawal and

how milestone payments would be treated.

       EDFps requests that the Commission direct MISO to implement concrete tracking and

accountability measures for facility studies – such as milestone reporting requirements and

enforceable timelines for MISO and Transmission Owners – as a necessary complement to the

withdrawal and restudy reforms already before the Commission.

IV.    CONCLUSION
       For the foregoing reasons, EDFps respectfully requests that the Commission accept

MISO’s LQA Proposal, including the penalty-free withdrawal opportunity at DP2 and the one-

restudy limit for DPP-2022 and subsequent DPP cycles. EDFps further requests that the

Commission (1) direct MISO to clarify Section 7.6.2.4 to cross-reference Section 5.15, (2)

require MISO to accelerate proposed reforms that separate DPP cycles, and (3) implement

concrete tracking and accountability measures for transmission facility studies. These additional

steps are necessary to achieve the accuracy and finality goals the LQA Proposal is designed to

achieve.

                                     Respectfully submitted,
